newsitem.title: UK: FUND VIEW - Invesco favours Hong Kong, Korea for 97.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Invesco favours Hong Kong, Korea for 97.

text.p: Foreign investor perceptions of Hong Kong and China are more pessimistic than those of local players but Invesco Asset Management will remain overweight as regards Hong Kong in 1997.

Asia chief investment officer Anna Tong said in an interview that the 130 million stg Invesco Asia investment trust would stick with Hong Kong, after 33 percent returns in dollar terms over 1996, in the run-up to the handover to China on July 1.
"It's on the back of the economic soft landing achieved in China and monetary policy there being relaxed," said Tong.
"Also, there has been a recovery in the residential property market in Hong Kong, with prices up 10-15 percent. That has helped the index, which has a 30 percent weighting in the sector."

She said foreign investors may have the jitters ahead of the takeover by Beijing, but local investors had been getting used to the idea since former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher first raised it in 1993.

"China deserves more credit than people have given it. It has confounded critics by managing a soft landing. And Hong Kong is now China's window to the West, where it has management skills and technology."

In London to speak to global portfolio investors, Tong said locals have done their background work and Hong Kong is increasingly linking up to the Chinese economy. "Manufacturing is already moving across to China to take advantage of the cheap leabour and growing markets there."

Hong Kong already directs some 60 percent of its foreign direct investment into China, while Chinese investors are heavily involved in the stock market, partly accounting for the leap in the property market.

Tong also sees Hong Kong, with its dollar-linked economy, surviving any rise in U.S. interest rates. "We see the US inflation risk as neutral and even if US rates were to rise by 25 or 50 basis points, Hong Kong should hold its own."

Invesco's favoured sectors are red chip stocks (Hong Kong controlled companies that derive most of their earnings from China), property developers, banks and some conglomerates such as Hutchinson Whampoa.
Tong sees the Hang Seng, now around 13,400, topping 15,000 by the end of 1997, once the 14,000 level is breached.
Korea is Invesco's emerging market pick for 1997, largely on the better value now available.

Sarah Bates, managing director of Invesco Asset Management in London, said the recent image of the country had largely been shaped by television coverage of labour unrest. "But the market has not really been driven down by this factor," she said.
Tong said Korea, the focus of Invesco's 33 million stg investment trust, was down 33 percent in the last year in dollar terms "on a barrage of bad news".
"Everyone has had a dreadful time there this year, but we have had a marginally less dreadful time than anyone else." The fund is still only at a 3.0 percent discount.
She said Korea's semiconductor industry, its steel plants, petrochemicals -- any export industry -- have been hit.
"But the labour strikes are not really the main problem -- it's the current account deficit and a drastic drop in earnings growth that is really affecting investors' view."

"The market is down so much there is a chance it will recover on an improvement in earnings growth and falling interest rates. It is very much underowned and valuations on almost any basis are below levels at the last cyclical bottom in 1992."
"We are not trying to shoot the lights out," added Bates, "But it is a simple trust to buy for the bounce."
